growth_signal.value: In September 2026 it was named as one of seven Australian startups that together raised $274.7 million in a single week, though HEO's own share of that total was not stated.

entry.idea: Governments and satellite operators cannot easily see how their satellites are actually doing once they are in orbit, so HEO Robotics visually monitors and photographs satellites and other space objects for them.
entry.lesson: When a fast-growing industry creates a blind spot that used to need expensive, government-built hardware to see, sell the missing visibility as a service instead of building new hardware from scratch.
entry.name: HEO Robotics

growth.reason: No revenue or user numbers were given, but the team has grown to about 47 people and the company was highlighted in a big week of Australian startup funding.

market.reason: Governments and defense agencies worldwide need to track objects in orbit, but this is a specialised market, not something every business needs.

tech.reason: Combining space imaging, orbital mechanics and government-grade trust is hard to build and would take a strong team years to match.

entry.twist: Instead of building its own fleet of camera satellites, it works through partners like Raytheon Australia to turn cameras already in orbit into a way of inspecting other spacecraft, which it calls 'space-cams'.
entry.who_pays: Government space agencies and defense organisations pay HEO to monitor and inspect satellites and other objects in orbit.
entry.why_now: More satellites are being launched every year, and if one breaks, drifts or is threatened, governments and militaries increasingly want to know exactly what happened to it.
